title: That Viral Photo of San Francisco NIMBYs Shows How Housing Is Winning
excerpt: Hot take: The opposition to the Marina Safeway project shows everything that is right about housing in San Francisco.
content_html:
You probably saw that viral picture from San Francisco Chronicle reporter Laura Waxmann showing a room full of people opposed to the construction of 848 new apartments on the site of a Safeway supermarket in San Francisco’s Marina District.

The reason that photo gained 10 million views isn’t hard to understand — it’s a perfect illustration of something we at YIMBY Action deal with all the time. Older, whiter, wealthier residents dominate public meetings, especially about proposals for new homes are in their backyards, a phenomenon well documented in books like Neighborhood Defenders.

The standard take on the internet seems to be “look how terrible everything still is and doesn’t San Francisco suck”. Even after all the work we’ve done and all the laws we’ve changed, it’s still the same NIMBYs showing up to kill housing. And I get that. After all, this photo was taken in Santa Ana in 2014, and you can’t tell me it’s not the same photo.

I don’t want to beat up on old people — wisdom and age go together — but opponents of new housing often skew closer to Mitch McConnell than they do AOC.1 One of YIMBYism’s big ideas is that for decades we have mistakenly prioritized the people in those photos instead of literally everyone else.

But there is a key thing that people keep missing about this photo of the Marina opponents. It was NOT taken at an official public hearing. No government agency is (officially) listening to these people! This picture is, in fact, a picture of people realizing they do not have the platform and power they once did. Thanks to California laws like AB 2011, SB 330, and the Density Bonus, this proposal is real and these people will not get the veto they are accustomed to over the Marina Safeway project.

You can see on their faces how well they are taking that — which is to say, not well at all. They wear the expressions of people who are used to getting what they want, and are angry that things may not work that way anymore.

On August 12, the San Francisco Planning Department will have to decide if that’s true. That’s the deadline for the department to determine whether the Safeway project qualifies for streamlining under AB 2011.

The law is clear, and this is supposed to be a non-political decision. But the pressure is coming anyway: NIMBYs wrote a legally dubious letter, and the Marina District’s supervisor pledged to fight this “so-called project”2 before putting his name on that absurd NIMBY plea.3 Meanwhile Mayor Daniel Lurie — boss of the department that is supposed to approve it — remains opposed. The mayor and the supervisor are taking those positions in no small part because every single person in that photo is someone capable of hosting a house party for an elected official — they all have time, energy, money, and access that, for instance, a young person in the Bayview might not have.

On the other hand, there is (finally) a loud, visible, vocal group of pro-housing voters. YIMBYs have got some excellent quotes in the papers and online.4 There’s even some polling that indicates the project is popular, as housing tends to be. And YIMBY Law has sent the city a formal letter reminding them that we will, in fact, sue if they pull some nonsense.

If the city follows the law, the Planning Department will announce by August 11th that the project qualifies under AB 2011 for streamlined approvals. The NIMBYs may sue, but they don’t have much to go on, and — faster than ever before — the project will get built. If not, well, see that letter that YIMBY Law sent that I mentioned above.

It is a truth universally acknowledged that a good bill passed in a state legislature will be attacked upon implementation.

This is the revolution that YIMBYs are orchestrating. Before this revolution, this project would never have been proposed. Now? In one of the wealthiest neighborhoods in one of the wealthiest cities, a 25-story building is on the verge of being permitted over the objections of some of the city’s most politically influential people. Booyah.

Recently, the pundits Matthew Yglesias and Jerusalem Demsas were riffing5 about whether America was in fact an oligarchy or not on The Argument podcast, and the basic summary was that it’s not technically an oligarchy if mediumly wealthy people who care a lot get their way most of the time.

Oligarchy or not, we all agree that it fucking sucks. And in less than two weeks, here in San Francisco, it might suck slightly less. I’m going to call that a win. NIMBYs are going to keep organizing to try to claw back our progress. And it’s up to us to keep outworking them.

Obscure community meetings used to be where housing went to die. Now they aren’t. I hate to be a bitch, but this is what democracy looks like.

Share

1

Not all insects are crickets, but all crickets are insects. Not all old people are NIMBYs, but pretty much all NIMBYs are old.

2

Apparently, Supervisor Sherill believed it was a fake project meant to be a starting point for negotiations instead of an actual development that actual people would build. Whoops!

3

His argument is that the law requires a certain percentage of the surrounding area to be for urban use, and that parks are in fact not an “urban use.” My park-loving, urbanite toddlers would beg to disagree.

4

For example, Brandon Powell, Bay Area organizing director for YIMBY Action, said it was “disappointing to see a supervisor who understands the depth of San Francisco’s housing crisis dig in his heels in opposition to a wonderful project which will provide homes for hundreds of current and future San Franciscans, including 86 affordable units [...] We need not only this project but many more like it.”

5

Demsas summarized: “When I consider the structure of power in American politics, it often cleaves along lines that have nothing to do with being a billionaire. Homeowners dominate land use politics, professional associations capture licensing rules, industry representatives shape low-salience regulations on their issues because few other people care enough to engage. All of this can produce profoundly unequal outcomes without being the work of a coherent oligarchic class.”

content_html_zh:
您可能看过《旧金山纪事报》记者劳拉·瓦克斯曼 (Laura Waxmann) 发布的一张广为人知的照片，照片中满屋子的人反对在旧金山滨海区的西夫韦超市工地上建造 848 套新公寓。

这张照片获得 1000 万浏览量的原因并不难理解——它完美地说明了我们 YIMBY Action 一直在处理的问题。 年长、白人、富裕的居民主导了公共会议，尤其是有关在自家后院建造新房的提案，这种现象在《邻里捍卫者》等书中有详细记录。

互联网上的标准看法似乎是“看看一切仍然多么糟糕，旧金山不是很糟糕吗”。 即使我们做了所有的工作并修改了所有的法律，但仍然有同样的邻避者出现来扼杀住房。 我明白了。 毕竟，这张照片是 2014 年在圣安娜拍摄的，你不能告诉我这不是同一张照片。

我不想打击老年人——智慧和年龄是相辅相成的——但新住房的反对者往往比 AOC 更接近米奇·麦康奈尔 (Mitch McConnell)。1 YIMBYism 的一大理念是，几十年来，我们错误地优先考虑了这些照片中的人，而不是其他所有人。

但关于玛丽娜对手的这张照片，人们一直忽略了一个关键的事情。 它不是在正式的公开听证会上采取的。 没有任何政府机构（正式）倾听这些人的声音！ 事实上，这张照片是人们意识到自己不再拥有曾经拥有的平台和权力的照片。 得益于 AB 2011、SB 330 和密度奖金等加州法律，该提案是真实的，这些人不会在 Marina Safeway 项目上获得他们所习惯的否决权。

你可以从他们的脸上看出他们对此的接受程度如何——也就是说，一点也不好。 他们的表情就像那些习惯了得到自己想要的东西的人一样，并对事情可能不再那样进行感到愤怒。

8 月 12 日，旧金山规划部门将不得不决定这是否属实。 这是该部门确定 Safeway 项目是否有资格根据 AB 2011 进行精简的最后期限。

法律是明确的，这应该是一个非政治决定。 但压力还是来了：邻避者写了一封法律上可疑的信，滨海区的主管承诺反对这个“所谓的项目”2，然后才将自己的名字写在那个荒谬的邻避请求上。3 与此同时，市长丹尼尔·卢里——本应批准该项目的部门负责人——仍然反对。 市长和主管担任这些职位在很大程度上是因为照片中的每个人都有能力为民选官员举办家庭聚会——他们都有时间、精力、金钱和访问权限，而这些是湾景区的年轻人可能没有的。

另一方面，（终于）出现了一群大声、明显、直言不讳的支持住房的选民。 YIMBY 在报纸和网上得到了一些精彩的引用。4 甚至有一些民意调查表明该项目很受欢迎，就像住房一样。 YIMBY Law 已向该市发出正式信函，提醒他们，如果他们胡言乱语，我们实际上将提起诉讼。

如果该市遵守法律，规划部门将在 8 月 11 日之前宣布该项目符合 AB 2011 的简化审批条件。 邻避者可能会提起诉讼，但他们没有什么可继续的，而且项目将以比以往更快的速度建成。 如果没有，请参阅我上面提到的 YIMBY Law 发送的那封信。

州议会通过的好法案，实施起来就会遭到攻击，这是举世公认的真理。

这就是 YIMBY 正在策划的一场革命。 在这场革命之前，这个项目永远不会被提出。 现在？ 在最富有的城市之一的最富有的社区之一，一栋 25 层的建筑即将获得批准，但该市一些最具政治影响力的人士表示反对。 嘘。

最近，专家马修·伊格莱西亚斯（Matthew Yglesias）和耶路撒冷·德姆萨斯（Jerusalem Demsas）在《争论》播客上反复讨论美国是否实际上是一个寡头政治，基本总结是，如果关心很多事情的中等富裕人士大多数时候都得偿所愿，那么从技术上讲，它就不是寡头政治。

无论寡头政治与否，我们都同意这很糟糕。 不到两周的时间，在旧金山，情况可能会稍微好一点。 我将称之为胜利。 邻避者将继续组织起来，试图夺回我们的进展。 我们有责任继续超越他们。

默默无闻的社区会议曾经是住房消亡的根源。 现在他们不是了。 我讨厌成为一个婊子，但这就是民主的样子。
